title: This Tiny World in Our Solar System Has Rings Like Saturn and James Webb Found They're Growing and Fading
excerpt: James Webb cannot see chariklo’s rings directly but their shadows revealed that something is happening to them.
content:
What if I told you that Saturn and the other gas giants are not the only worlds in our Solar System to sport rings?

Between Saturn and Uranus, a small icy body just 250 kilometers (155 miles) across carries two narrow rings of its own. It is called Chariklo, and it belongs to a strange class of objects known as Centaurs, which orbit the Sun among the giant planets. When astronomers discovered its rings in 2013, Chariklo became the first small Solar System body known to possess such a system.

Now those rings have delivered another surprise.

The James Webb Space Telescope has found evidence that Chariklo’s rings are changing on timescales of just a few years. Its dense inner ring has become substantially more opaque, while the much fainter outer ring appears to have faded.

Webb cannot directly see either ring. They are too narrow, too distant, and too close to Chariklo. Instead, astronomers watched the rings briefly blot out the light of a distant star as Chariklo passed in front of it on Oct. 18, 2022—a method known as stellar occultation.

Those fleeting shadows may now let astronomers track how Chariklo’s ring system changes over time.

Seeing Rings That Webb Cannot See

Centaurs are small, icy objects whose orbits weave among the giant planets. They occupy a kind of middle ground between asteroids and comets.

Chariklo, though, turned out to be unusual even by Centaur standards. It has two rings circling it at radii of roughly 390 and 405 kilometers (242 and 252 miles) from its center. Astronomers discovered them during another stellar occultation in 2013, a finding described in the original Nature study the following year.

×

Until then, rings were known only around the Solar System’s four gas giants. Since then, astronomers have found ring systems around other small bodies, including Haumea and Quaoar.

Webb offered a new way to scrutinize Chariklo. The 2022 event became the first stellar occultation by a small Solar System body successfully observed with JWST—and the first recorded from beyond Earth’s orbit. NASA published an early account of the observation in 2023, before the full analysis was complete.

The geometry was almost absurdly precise. The star’s apparent path missed Chariklo’s surface by only about 7.4 kilometers. Chariklo moved relative to Webb at just 2.5 kilometers per second, unusually slowly for an occultation. Webb recorded the scene about 3.3 times each second, giving the researchers a spatial sampling of roughly 750 meters along the star’s path.

That precision exposed a surprise.

The inner ring, called C1R, had an average opacity of about 0.30 in pre-Webb measurements. Webb measured about 0.43. Its equivalent width—a measure combining how wide and opaque the ring appears—increased by roughly 50%. The difference is statistically significant.

The outer ring, C2R, went the other way. Its equivalent width in the Webb observations was about 60% lower than in 2017. Webb barely detected it at 1.5 micrometers and did not detect it at 3.2 micrometers.

The Lives of Rings

The obvious explanation would be that material migrated from the outer ring into the inner one. But the numbers do not work. The increase measured in C1R was about 10 times larger than the material apparently lost from C2R.

Instead, collisions among larger particles could have produced clouds of smaller fragments, increasing the inner ring’s effective opacity. The outer ring may be losing fine grains, which radiation pressure can gradually push onto unstable orbits. A still-undetected shepherd moonlet could also help confine or replenish the rings.

Chariklo may not be alone. A 2025 study of the Centaur Chiron found structures that had changed across decades of occultations, leading researchers to suggest they might be witnessing another ring system forming and evolving. And planetary rings themselves are not immutable: Saturn’s dusty rings, Neptune’s arcs and Uranus’s faint rings have all shown changes with time.

There is still an important caveat. Webb observed at infrared wavelengths, while many earlier measurements used visible light. Different particle sizes and compositions can block different wavelengths by different amounts. Modeling indicates that this effect alone cannot explain C1R’s increase, but the weaker outer ring remains less certain.

A future visible-light occultation could settle the question.

“Our results force us to rethink how they form, how they evolve, and what mechanisms maintain their stability,” Pablo Santos-Sanz, the study’s lead author at the Institute of Astrophysics of Andalusia, said in an IAA-CSIC statement. “The ability to detect these changes opens a new window for understanding the evolution of these systems and, possibly, that of other ring systems in the Solar System.”

For now, Chariklo’s rings remain invisible to Webb itself. But whenever they happen to cross a distant star, their shadows can reveal a ring system that is very much alive.

The study was published in the journal Science Advances.
